design_detail: Retrospective, repeated annual analysis of aggregate data from the National Poison Data System (NPDS), the database of the American Association of Poison Control Centers that records potentially toxic exposures reported to the 55 regional poison control centres serving the United States and its territories (Pediatrics 2023;151(2):e2022057761; article pages 1 to 7). Cases: calls coded with the generic code for edible cannabis in children younger than 6 years, 2017 to 2021 (2021 data preliminary). Reported: counts by year; age, sex, place of exposure, management site and caller site; the NPDS medical outcome (no, minor, moderate or major effect); level of care; the top 30 clinical effects and top 20 treatments among the 4,827 cases followed to a known outcome; and chi-squared comparisons of 2017 to 2019 (before the COVID-19 pandemic) with 2020 to 2021. No denominator of children exposed and no comparison group. Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as for the surveillance series sc_jones_2015.
can_establish: How many calls about children younger than 6 who ate cannabis edibles reached US poison centres each year from 2017 to 2021, and what share of all calls about children of that age they were; the ages, sex and place of exposure of those children; how the reported cases were graded (no, minor, moderate or major effect), which clinical effects and treatments were recorded among those followed up, and what level of care they received, year by year.
cannot_establish: How many children ate edibles (only reported calls reach the data, which the authors call an underestimate) or the rate per child in the population; why the calls rose (no state-level data, so the link the authors draw with legalization of adult use is not tested here, and more reporting or less stigma could contribute, as they say); whether the pandemic itself made cases more severe (the 2017 to 2019 against 2020 to 2021 comparison sets earlier against later years of a series already rising, with a coding change in 2019 and changing choices of where children were treated); what was eaten, how much THC, from what source or in what packaging (not in these data); outcomes for the 30% not followed to a known outcome; and any effect after the acute episode.

sample.recruitment: All cases in the NPDS data portal with the generic code for edible cannabis in children younger than 6, 2017 to 2021: calls to US poison centres from homes, health care facilities and other places (Methods › Data Source and Case Selection Criteria, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age under 6 years; edible cannabis code; years 2017 to 2021. The code is not named, and the paper does not say whether cases were limited to unintentional exposures or to exposures to cannabis alone, though it describes them as unintentional ingestions. The 2,216 cases not followed to a known outcome were left out of the analysis of clinical effects and treatments (Methods › Clinical Effects and Therapies, pp. 2-3).
sample.demographics: Median age 3 years (interquartile range 2 to 4): under 1 year 136 (1.9%), 1 year 1,046 (14.9%), 2 years 1,954 (27.7%), 3 years 1,734 (24.6%), 4 years 1,265 (18.0%), 5 years 891 (12.7%), unknown 17 (0.2%). Female 3,450 (49.0%), male 3,495 (49.6%), unknown 98 (1.4%) (Results › General Characteristics, 1st paragraph, p. 3; Table 1, p. 4).
sample.attrition: Not followed to a known outcome: 2,141 (30.4%) in Table 1; the Methods leave 2,216 out of the clinical analyses, apparently counting the 74 confirmed non-exposures with them (see reporting issues). Level of care: 2,268 (32.2%) lost to follow-up or other, 625 (8.9%) refused referral or did not arrive at a health care facility.
sample.selection_effects: Passive surveillance: only exposures someone reported to a poison centre, and reporting may have changed over the years (the authors name more reporting and less stigma as possible contributors). 43.6% of calls came from a health care facility, so cases already seen by clinicians are well represented, while mild cases handled at home may be missed. No state is identified.

exposure.measurement: A child's eating of a cannabis edible as reported by the caller and coded by poison-centre staff with the NPDS generic code; 74 cases were coded as confirmed non-exposures. No laboratory confirmation is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not in the data analysed: product, amount and THC content are unknown. The Introduction's background on adult servings and multi-serving packages is cited from other sources, not measured here.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: the paper does not say whether calls involving other substances were included or left out.

comparison.controls: None. Comparisons are between years and between 2017 to 2019 and 2020 to 2021; the yearly share uses all calls about children under 6 as its denominator (956,871 in 2017 and 846,296 in 2021, Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No child-level data beyond age and sex; state, product type, amount eaten, time to care and other substances are not available; changes in reporting over time were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: NPDS coding by poison-centre staff: the medical outcome categories defined in the NPDS coding manual (cited, not read; not defined in the paper), clinical-effect and treatment codes, and level of health care facility.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard national coding, but in 2019 the codes for decreased mental status (drowsiness or lethargy, coma) were replaced by graded CNS depression; the authors combined the codes into one CNS depression category. The data depend on what callers and clinicians report (Methods, p. 3; limitations, p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: Severity as the NPDS medical outcome (no, minor, moderate or major effect), as a share of all 7,043 cases; level of care as admitted to critical care, admitted to noncritical care, treated and released, refused referral or did not arrive, lost to follow-up or other; clinical effects and treatments as shares of the 4,827 cases followed to a known outcome.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. At least 12 chi-squared comparisons are reported (yearly share; four outcome grades; three levels of care; CNS depression, tachycardia, vomiting, respiratory depression), each only as P < .05 or P > .05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; coding by poison-centre staff at the time of the call.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and percentages only; no confidence intervals, test statistics or exact P values. Rise 2017 to 2021: 207 to 3,054 calls (printed 1375.0%; editors' arithmetic 1375.4%, 14.75 times), and 0.2 to 3.6 per 1,000 calls about children under 6 (Figure 1 data labels 0.2, 0.6, 1.1, 2.5 and 3.6 for 2017 to 2021). 2017 to 2019 against 2020 to 2021: major effect 1.6% against 2.4%; moderate 15.9% against 23.8%; minor 33.4% against 30.1%; no effect 17% against 11.8%; critical care 6.6% against 8.6%; noncritical admission 12.7% against 15.7% (the yearly shares in Table 2 give 11.2% for 2017 to 2019, editors' arithmetic); treated and released 41.2% against 34.5%; CNS depression 61.6% against 72.9%; vomiting 7.5% against 10.0% (each P < .05); tachycardia 10.3% against 11.6% and respiratory depression 2.5% against 3.3% (P > .05).
analysis.covariates: None; no adjustment of any kind.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the institutional review board judged the study exempt (deidentified data that the paper calls publicly available).
analysis.selective_reporting: Clinical effects limited to the top 30 codes (with codes of the 'other' organ systems removed) and treatments to the top 20; denominators of cases followed up in each period are not given; counts by state were not available.
analysis.power: Not addressed; counts are large in the pandemic years and small in 2017 (207).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Calls about young children who ate cannabis edibles rose every year from 2017 to 2021, in number and as a share of all calls about children under 6, while those calls overall fell. Most children were 1 to 4 years old and had eaten the product at home. About a quarter of all cases (about a third of those followed up) were graded moderate or major, 22.7% were admitted, 35 were intubated and no deaths were reported. Severity and admission shares were higher in 2020 to 2021 than in 2017 to 2019.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say the exposures 'can cause significant toxicity' and are responsible for an increasing number of hospitalizations, which the counts support for reported cases. The Discussion links the rise to more states allowing adult recreational use, as a belief, which cannot be tested without state data, as the authors acknowledge, and names the pandemic as a possible part. The period comparison is presented as rising severity during the pandemic, but compares later with earlier years of a rising series, across a coding change and changing choices of where children were treated; the authors themselves say it is unknown why disposition changed. The abstract has three errors (97.7% residential for 97.1%; the number treated and released is said to have decreased when the share fell and the number rose; the sentence on major and moderate effects reverses the periods). The prevention measures in the Conclusions are recommendations, not tested here.

timeline.event: RTI Press overview of edibles reports second-hand that US poison-centre calls about cannabis in young children rose from 2005 to 2011, with similar rises in edible calls in 2013 to 2015, and says emergency visits for children remained relatively low.
Cao et al., Clinical Toxicology: edible cannabis exposures reported to US poison centres (cited as this paper's reference 3; not read).
American College of Medical Toxicology position statement on paediatric cannabis exposure (cited as reference 16; not read); the authors note that calls kept rising after it.

replication.where_it_stands: National data in the same direction as the earlier state-level reports the paper cites (not read here). None of these sources can separate legal sales, product changes, the pandemic and reporting as causes of the rise.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have indicated they have no potential conflicts of interest to disclose (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are affiliated with the Illinois Poison Center; also Southern Illinois University School of Medicine (Tweet), Rush University Medical Center (Nemanich) and NorthShore University HealthSystem (Wahl). Dr Wahl conceived the study, obtained the NPDS data and did the statistical analyses (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: State-level poison-centre and emergency-department data with child population denominators, dates of legal retail sales, product type and amount, and measures of reporting behaviour, analysed as interrupted time series, would show how much of the rise follows legal sales or product changes rather than reporting or the pandemic.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: NPDS covers calls to all 55 US poison centres, the right frame for reported exposures; it misses exposures never reported, which the authors call an underestimate.
A census of coded cases, but the code is not named, and whether only unintentional or only cannabis-alone exposures were taken is not stated.
7,043 cases; 4,827 followed to a known outcome.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, place of exposure, management and caller site; no state, product, amount or other substances.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 30.4% not followed to a known outcome; clinical effects and treatments analysed only among those followed, while the severity grades in Table 1 are shares of all cases; whether follow-up differed by year is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Exposure from the caller's account, coded by poison-centre staff; no laboratory confirmation reported; 74 confirmed non-exposures recorded.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: National coding manual; the 2019 change in the CNS depression codes was handled by combining categories; outcome grades depend on follow-up.

Only P < .05 or P > .05 reported, with no test statistics or intervals and no correction across at least 12 comparisons; the before-and-during-pandemic split confounds a rising trend with the pandemic; the Discussion's 295.7% is the ratio of the two periods' counts, not the increase (195.7%), and the periods differ in length (three years against two).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Reporting to poison centres is voluntary; the share of exposures reported, and whether it changed over the years, is unknown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of reported calls about young children who ate cannabis edibles, the counts, ages, places and graded outcomes are national and internally consistent in the tables, but they are floors, and part of the rise may reflect reporting. The statistical comparisons are thinly reported and the pandemic contrast cannot isolate the pandemic. Citable for the yearly counts and shares, ages, place of exposure, level of care and graded outcomes among reported cases; not for incidence per child, for the causes of the rise (legal sales, the pandemic or reporting), or for a pandemic effect on severity.

key_findings.finding: 7,043 calls, 2017 to 2021: 207 in 2017, 590 in 2018, 983 in 2019, 2,209 in 2020 and 3,054 in 2021 (an increase the paper gives as 1375.0%). Edible calls were 0.02% of all calls about children under 6 in 2017 (0.2 per 1,000) and 0.36% in 2021 (3.6 per 1,000; P < .05); the data labels of Figure 1 give 0.2, 0.6, 1.1, 2.5 and 3.6 per 1,000 for 2017 to 2021.
key_findings.locator: Results › General Characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Figure 1, data labels (p. 3); Table 1, Number of cases per year (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: (3,054 - 207)/207 = 1375.4%, 14.75 times. The largest rise in number was 2019 to 2020 (+1,226, printed as +124.7%, which the Discussion calls the biggest increase); the largest relative rise was 2017 to 2018 (+185.0%).

key_findings.finding: Over the same five years, all calls about children aged 0 to 5 to poison centres fell from 956,871 to 846,296.

Ages: median 3 years (interquartile range 2 to 4); 2-year-olds were the largest group (1,954, 27.7%), then 3-year-olds (1,734, 24.6%), 4-year-olds (1,265, 18.0%), 1-year-olds (1,046, 14.9%), 5-year-olds (891, 12.7%) and under 1 year (136, 1.9%). Female 3,450 (49.0%), male 3,495 (49.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results › General Characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Age and Sex (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Place: own residence 6,391 (90.7%), another residence 451 (6.4%), other or unknown 201 (2.9%); residential in all 6,842 (97.1%; the abstract says 97.7%). Managed on site without referral 973 (13.8%); already in or on the way to a health care facility when the centre was called 3,405 (48.3%); referred by the centre 2,557 (36.3%). Callers: a health care facility 3,071 (43.6%), a residence 3,468 (49.2%), other places 7.2%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); Results › General Characteristics, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Exposure site and Management site (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Medical outcome of all 7,043: major effect 155 (2.2%), moderate 1,539 (21.9%), minor 2,211 (31.4%), no effect 923 (13.1%), confirmed non-exposure 74 (1.1%), not followed to a known outcome 2,141 (30.4%). No deaths were reported in the five years.
key_findings.locator: Results › Medical Outcome, paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Medical outcome (p. 4); Results › Clinical Effects by Organ System › Respiratory Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: moderate or major 1,694, 24.1% of all calls and 35.1% of the 4,827 followed to a known outcome; major 3.2% of those.

key_findings.finding: Level of care: admitted to critical care 573 (8.1%), to noncritical care 1,027 (14.6%), together 22.7% as in the abstract; treated and released 2,550 (36.2%); refused referral or did not arrive 625 (8.9%); lost to follow-up or other 2,268 (32.2%).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); Results › Disposition, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, Level of HCF (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Year by year (Table 2, % of each year's calls, 2017 to 2021): critical care 8.7, 4.7, 7.3, 8.2, 9.0; noncritical care 9.7, 10.5, 12.0, 14.9, 16.3; treated and released 44.9, 42.4, 39.7, 32.6, 35.9. Text: critical care 6.6% in 2017 to 2019 against 8.6% in 2020 to 2021 (a 30% increase), noncritical care 12.7% against 15.7%, treated and released 41.2% against 34.5% (each P < .05).
key_findings.note: Weighting the yearly shares in Table 2 by the yearly counts gives 11.2% (not 12.7%) for noncritical care in 2017 to 2019, while reproducing the 1,027 total and the 15.7% for 2020 to 2021 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Severity by period, 2017 to 2019 (1,780 calls) against 2020 to 2021 (5,263): major effect 1.6% against 2.4%, moderate 15.9% against 23.8%, minor 33.4% against 30.1%, no effect 17% against 11.8% (each P < .05); CNS depression 61.6% against 72.9% (P < .05); vomiting 7.5% against 10.0% (P < .05); tachycardia 10.3% against 11.6% and respiratory depression 2.5% against 3.3% (both P > .05).
key_findings.locator: Results › Medical Outcome, paragraph (p. 3); Results › Clinical Effects by Organ System: Neurologic, Cardiovascular and Gastrointestinal Effects (p. 4), Respiratory Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Clinical effects among the 4,827 followed to a known outcome: CNS depression 3,381 (70.0%), major CNS depression or coma 90 (1.9%), tachycardia 548 (11.4%), vomiting 458 (9.5%), ataxia 359 (7.4%), agitation 342 (7.1%), confusion 294 (6.1%), mydriasis 284 (5.9%), respiratory depression 148 (3.1%), hypotension 123 (2.5%), seizure 79 (1.6%), bradycardia 68 (1.4%), hallucinations or delusions 47 (1.0%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical Effects by Organ System (p. 4 and p. 5); Table 3 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Treatments among the 4,827: intravenous fluids 997 (20.7%), dilution or washing 525 (10.9%), food or snack 495 (10.3%), oxygen 193 (4.0%), benzodiazepines 107 (2.2%), single-dose charcoal 100 (2.1%), naloxone 68 (1.4%), intubation 35 (0.7%), ventilator 33 (0.7%), vasopressors 13 (0.3%); the authors put intubation at about 1 in 140 children.
key_findings.locator: Results › Therapies, paragraph (p. 5); Table 4 (p. 5); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Authors' explanations: the number of cases per state could not be determined; the increases are believed to be associated with more states allowing adult recreational use; COVID-related quarantines and school or daycare closures may have played a part (the 2020 to 2021 count was 5,263 against 1,780 in 2017 to 2019). For the change in disposition they say it is unknown why it occurred, and suggest clinicians' comfort and experience, bed availability, more THC per package or more products bought, or more severe effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 5, continued on p. 6); Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: only exposures reported to US poison centres, so the numbers underestimate the actual number; unknown whether more reporting or less stigma contributed to the rise; data depend on what patients, families and health care staff report and on coding by poison-centre staff; missing data and loss to follow-up limit the picture of effects and outcomes.

Methods: aggregate NPDS data, generic code for edible cannabis, children under 6, 2017 to 2021 (2021 preliminary); 2,216 cases not followed to a known outcome excluded from the clinical analyses, leaving 4,827; top 30 clinical effects (other-organ-system codes removed) and top 20 treatments; decreased-mental-status codes replaced by graded CNS depression in 2019 and combined; chi-squared tests of yearly volume and of 2017 to 2019 against 2020 to 2021.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Source; Case Selection Criteria; General Characteristics Data; Medical Outcome; Disposition; Clinical Effects and Therapies (p. 2, continued on p. 3)

key_findings.finding: No external funding; the authors declare no potential conflicts of interest. All three authors are affiliated with the Illinois Poison Center.
key_findings.locator: Author affiliations and contributions (p. 1); Funding and Conflict of Interest Disclosures (p. 7)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 97.7% of exposures occurred in a residential setting; the Results give 6,842 cases (97.1%), which matches Table 1 (6,391 + 451 of 7,043 = 97.15%, editors' arithmetic).

The Discussion calls the change from 1,780 cases (2017 to 2019) to 5,263 (2020 to 2021) an increase of 295.7%; 5,263 is 295.7% of 1,780, an increase of 195.7%, and the periods are three years against two (per year, about 593 against 2,632, about 4.4 times; editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite 295.7% as the increase; give the yearly counts instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives noncritical admissions as 12.7% of cases in 2017 to 2019 (a 24% rise to 15.7%), but the yearly shares in Table 2 weighted by the yearly counts give 11.2% (editors' arithmetic); the same weighting reproduces the 1,027 total in Table 1, the 15.7% for 2020 to 2021, and the text's critical-care (6.6%, 8.6%) and treated-and-released (41.2%, 34.5%) shares.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2017 to 2019 noncritical share is probably 11.2%, a relative rise of about 40%, not 24%.

reporting_issues.issue: Numbers and shares are mixed up in places: the abstract says the number of patients treated and released decreased between periods, but only the share fell (41.2% to 34.5%; the count implied by Table 2 rose from about 733 to about 1,817, editors' arithmetic); the text says the number admitted to noncritical care increased 68.0% from 9.7% in 2017 to 16.3% in 2021, which is the rise in the share (the count rose from about 20 to about 498). The abstract's sentence on major and moderate effects puts the periods the wrong way round.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite shares as shares; the absolute numbers rose in every category.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods exclude 2,216 cases not followed to a known outcome and analyse 4,827; Table 1 has 2,141 not followed plus 74 confirmed non-exposures (2,215) and 4,828 cases in the four known-outcome grades.
reporting_issues.consequence: A difference of one case; the 4,827 evidently exclude the confirmed non-exposures as well.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor items: minor effects are 31.3% in the text and 31.4% in Table 1, and the period shares for minor effects (33.4% and 30.1%) imply about 2,179 cases against 2,211 (editors' arithmetic); flumazenil is 0.2% in the text and 0.1% in Table 4 (7 of 4,827); the text says Table 4 lists 23 treatments, and it lists 22; caller-site figures are attributed to Table 1, which does not show them; 1375.0% is 1375.4% by the editors' arithmetic.
reporting_issues.consequence: None changes a conclusion; they show the text was not checked against the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Statistical reporting: every comparison is given only as P < .05 or P > .05, with no test statistic, degrees of freedom or interval and no correction across at least 12 comparisons; the before-and-during-pandemic contrast compares three earlier with two later years of a series that was already rising (207, 590, 983).
reporting_issues.consequence: Period differences show that later years differed from earlier ones, not that the pandemic caused them.
